transcriptText:
Hi everyone. Uh my name is Johannes um
Galatano. So perfect pronunciation. Uh
I'm CEO co-founder of the fraction and
uh I'm here to talk about earth
observation. Um so
I want to tell you a little bit about
how we started uh our journey and we
started it building um actually a
camera. So this camera is the um
research that came out of um MIT and UMD
research together with co-founder Sikad
Guha who's a professor at UMD and MIT
and um we had this camera and we thought
hey this has some very cool properties.
So first of all it replaces your uh
normal camera and your onboard
processing like a GPU and you can do two
very cool things. one, you can see
beyond the defraction limit, which means
with the same type of lens, you can see
it 20 times further. But also, you can
process information about a thousand
times faster, which is kind of the model
we saw with quantum processing here. And
um, you know, we started with this kind
of research and thought, well, you know,
there's a lot of applications for this,
right? So, you could build drones, you
could build robots, you could build uh
manufacturing, right? There's lots of
applications, even automotive. So you
kind of can guess what we chose to do. I
mean looking at our booth over there and
since the space conference we decided to
do earth observation. Um so at least to
start with earth observation and we have
this little guy here. Um this is uh
Galileo 1 named after my co-founder's
dog Galileo not after the scientist but
also the first astronomer ever. And um
this here is the highest resolution
earth observation satellite in the
world. Um that's commercially available.
uh this can see this little desk here
from low earth orbit. Now
when we pitch this idea to uh different
people you know when you have a good
idea you go out and talk to people and
say hey is this a good idea or are we
going down the wrong path right? So when
we pitched this to people we got very
interesting comments. So one comment was
well can you actually earn more money
from doing earth observation than it
costs to build the thing right the
satellite because the satellite is
expensive.
Then somebody said this like one of the
venture capitalists told s well is
planet even making money like what kind
of industry are you going into right
like if the leader cannot even make
money with this um and then there's this
company which we really admire too
similar like planet albido um it's a
startup from YC um they did vio and
started with 10 cm resolution and then
you know they pivoted recently in this
year so they said well why did these
guys pivot and you guys going to earth
observation right um and then we heard
this so one VC told us earth obser
observation is dead. So um we were you
know wondering is this actually true and
is earth observation dead? Well we
looked at the use cases and thinking
about earth observation. Earth
observation is critical for
infrastructure. So our infrastructure
inspections rely on having earth
observation and inspecting from space
but also agriculture relies on
increasing um yield but also predicting
things like past and other issues.
Trading and um agriculture companies
rely on how much to plant, how much to
buy and how to sell. But also obviously
security and resiliency um is
unthinkable without earth observation
which is where we started right. So
without earth observation we are blind
on a planetary scale. So clearly the use
case is very interesting is very
critical. So where's the problem right?
Well the problem is that when you look
at something you need to get data from
the ground obviously light you need to
get the light up on the satellite then
the satellite has to send the data back
to earth so you can do something with
it. So you have a slow latency and then
you need to process this data. Right now
the problem was that only 10% of data is
being processed on on orbit or 10% of
the data that is captured is actually
sent back to earth. So that means
there's a big problem of processing on
orbit and we heard actually in the
previous talk too this is a big issue.
So this is very much um uh on point.
Now what did the customers want? We
talked to the customers. So what do you
want? First of all they wanted to have
um higher quality signals. So we have
moved away from images right people
don't care about images they said well
we have terabytes and millions and
millions of images that we get but
honestly I don't have a whole department
that just looks into each image and then
you have 50 companies all are doing the
same thing so obviously you need to
aggregate this then we also want to have
a much faster insight right so space is
very slow from actually from tasking a
satellite you need about six hours to
even get the satellite in the in the
right place and then you need another 6
hours to get the data down even in the
best case. Now these actions need to
come sometimes in seconds or below
especially in security use cases and in
that case um the the space doesn't even
work right you need drones you need
other applications that give you much
faster insight and then you also need
reliability I mean every day there is
actually war happening up in space that
there's spoofing there's other
activities um there is proximity
operations right so it doesn't mean that
you have a satellite up there you
actually get the data and have some
operational capability.

images to decisions. So originally you
used to have just images where were
pixels right? So you have pixels in
there. Oops. Which give you an image
like that. Now this is a busy port but
what's going on in the port? I don't
want to know get a pretty image. I want
to know what is going on in that port.
How are things moving? Where are the
ships going? How much oil, iron, and
other inventory do they carry? how often
do they come in and I want to take
decisions. So I want this to be
integrated downstream in my decision
making so that I can take instant
decisions with this and space wasn't
built around that because we know that
the winners so far have been people who
built and collected a lot of pixels from
a lot of satellites and a lot of images.
But that paradigm has shifted completely
because of customer expectations. Right?
In the '9s this used to be a good
business. Not anymore.
Now what do you need to overcome? One,
sensors. Um, so you need better sensors
that can do actually capture more data
and different kind of data you can
aggregate. So our main IP as mentioned
was the camera, right? So I can here
advertise a little bit again from our
company but obviously our quantum sensor
um provides data that is not providable
by other sensors. So obviously you need
innovation there. Secondly, um you also
need to update the ground infrastructure
because you want to have that input to
come instantaneously or real time down
to earth. So you need a proliferated
ground um uh capabilities to downstream
this kind of data. And there's been
actually another startup here that has
been very successful in doing that. And
then of course you need onorbit compute.
Uh that's a data center in space. Um so
Philip Johnson, good friend, he built
this very cool company. Um and there's
obviously other cool companies that
built this among others Google and
Nvidia and so on that want to do this
but um this is a capability that is
direly required to get all this data
processed and down from orbit.

observation? We think a couple
predictions. One, aggregation. So we
think aggregation is king in the sense
that when you have platforms like uh
Skyfi or UP42 or so that get images from
and data sources from different
providers and different satellite
constellations and then provide it to
different end customers. That's a great
model. Um that's actually one of the
main reasons we thought hey let's go to
into this market because then the
frontfacing the customerf facing market
is already kind of captured by
aggregators right it's kind of the Uber
Eats concept right you open a restaurant
you already know all the customers will
find you on the app similar concept here
very cool um then models so how do you
aggregate that stuff and just beyond
images generate interesting insights you
run models my background is AI. I spent
my entire career in AI and I know the
power of these kinds of models. I didn't
do it in space. I've done it in many
other industries in physical AI and
drones. But in space, it's the same
paradigm, right? So, you have things
from DeepMind like Alpha Earth. If you
haven't seen it, check it out. Very
cool. Um IBM and NASA brought out a very
cool uh also public uh publicly
available model uh that aggregates
different modalities into insights.
And then lastly, people care. Again, the
customer cares now about real time
insights and outcomes, which means that
the whole industry needs to shift
towards giving them actional outcomes.
And we think again no single
constellation will win this. Obviously,
we're bringing out our own
constellation. If you know want to find
out more about that, we have a booth
over there. But um no single
constellation will win this, but an
aggregation of different modalities.
Now talking to the industry obviously
here is a bit represented obviously not
everybody does earth observation
[snorts] um but we think that first what
I know from my background in data and AI
working different industries was
standards and interoperability which
means my data needs to work with your
data and with Capella's data and with
other people in the room and we need to
be able to work and understand what
everybody else is doing so we can
synthesize data for the models
downstream. So that's what you do with
standards. And then interoperability
means um also my sensor works with um a
different payload. It might work with a
different cube set. It might work with a
hosted payload. How does this data come
from the hosted payload down? How do I
translate that? So all of that is under
interoperability.
Then partnerships. I think we talked we
heard also in the morning a lot about
partnerships. Partnerships are crucial
because again there's multiple parts.
For example, in this example, I like
just picking this guy up. Um, we have
the camera which we build. Then we buy a
telescope and we buy a bus, right? So
there's different parts of it. There's a
layer of streaming data down. So these
are all partners that we partner with to
make this a reality. And without this
ecosystem, I wouldn't be standing here.
Our company wouldn't be doing space. We
probably doing robotics, which was the
second, or industrial automation. um but
we wouldn't be here doing space. So
these partnerships are crucial and we'd
love to expand on these partnerships and
build with you all on expanding this.
And lastly for disruptors um you know
don't be afraid of space. I think that's
a personal story like um we started
obviously with DARPA and NASA that
sponsored this research for 10 years. Um
so it was kind of you know the next step
to go to space but again not
selfexplainable that we would end up in
space too. Um but uh this was an image
generated by uh um there was these
little LinkedIn aggregators that post
about space news and they created this
AI image for us. So that's why it looks
a bit wonky. But we think there's pretty
cool sensors out there and technologies
that haven't made it to space because uh
well people are afraid of that and you
would hear these comments once you start
raising even if you think oh space would
be a cool market to start with.

observation dead? Um yes, earth
observation is dead. But earth
intelligence is not and earth
intelligence is crucial for both the
mission, for our infrastructure, for
security and resiliency and for being
ahead of the game. We need to transition
into earth intelligence.
And that one for in my mind means real
time decision making from powered from
space and that's what we think is the
future of earth observation. So thank
you guys. Um come over to the booth if
you want to learn more about the tech
and thank you so much.
